question: Your answer linked the report that NVIDIA has been negotiating to guarantee OpenAI's lease of a large Ohio data center to the open thesis on the amount of credit support NVIDIA has extended. Why did you not open a thesis on whether NVIDIA signs that guarantee by a check date?
reply:
I linked it rather than opening a thesis because clean-1 already tracks "the amount of signed credit-support, guarantee, or similar credit-enhancement commitments NVIDIA discloses for AI cloud partners under the new model" by 2027-12-31, and section 3 says: "A new thesis that asks the same underlying question, about the same subject and scope, as an open thesis or another new thesis is not proposed: link its evidence to that thesis," and "Do not open a thesis about ... another estimate, source or wording of what an open thesis tracks." A separate yes/no on the Ohio guarantee also fails "why_a_separate_bet": both answers move together. Against that I weighed binding_obligation ("one not yet signed by whether it is signed by a check date within 18 months") and its date rule, plus the rumour tier — The Information's undated "recently been negotiating," quoting no signature.

An experienced analyst would log the Ohio guarantee as the largest single pipeline item under clean-1, press management on signature terms and tenor, and watch the 10-Q guarantee disclosures — not create a duplicate card.

question: Your answer linked the report that NVIDIA has been negotiating to guarantee OpenAI's lease of a large Ohio data center to the open thesis on the amount of credit support NVIDIA has extended. Why did you not open a thesis on whether NVIDIA signs that guarantee by a check date?
reply:
I treated it as covered, not separate: section 3 says an unsigned guarantee opens "by whether it is signed by a check date within 18 months of the item" — but also that "if an open thesis exists and its answer cannot move apart from it," you "link the evidence to every open thesis it informs instead," and "a question no date can settle is rewritten or not opened." The item gives no signing date, no guarantee size (the $500 billion is build-out cost), and the negotiation is unnamed-source. Weighed against: "A missing amount, date or scale never drops an item on its own."

An experienced analyst would keep this under clean-1 as rumour, note it as the largest potential contingent item, and watch for a filing disclosing the guarantee — arguably grounds for a separate signed-by check date.

question: Your answer linked the report that NVIDIA has been negotiating to guarantee OpenAI's lease of a large Ohio data center to the open thesis on the amount of credit support NVIDIA has extended. Why did you not open a thesis on whether NVIDIA signs that guarantee by a check date?
reply:
I weighed two instructions. Section 3: propose a thesis only when "no open thesis already asks it," and "A new thesis that asks the same underlying question, about the same subject and scope, as an open thesis... is not proposed: link its evidence to that thesis." Also: "Before proposing a new thesis... why an analyst would bet on the two separately because their answers can move apart... If the two cannot move apart, link the evidence."

Against those I weighed the OpenAI sentence itself: it gives no amount for NVIDIA's guarantee — "$500 billion" is the data center's build-out cost, not NVIDIA's commitment — and clean-1 already asks the total credit support NVIDIA commits to cloud partners. Signing it simply raises that total, so the two cannot move apart.

An experienced analyst would log it as an unconfirmed, unsigned candidate guarantee, flag signing as an increment to clean-1's total, and watch 8-Ks rather than bet separately.

question: Your answer opened one thesis on the big four hyperscalers' combined data-center capital expenditure for calendar 2026, and used the article's figure for calendar 2027 only as its reference. Why did you not open calendar 2027's combined spending as a thesis of its own?
reply:
Because a single thesis can hold only "one quantity for one period," and the request treats the 2027 figure as the same aggregate: "Another population or wording of the same aggregate is evidence for it," and do not open "another estimate, source or wording of what an open thesis tracks." Only "this or next calendar year" opens a shared_quantity, so 2026 was the eligible plan; the $1 trillion is NVIDIA's own projection — "a forecast is a statement, not a completed outcome" — not a hyperscaler decision. I weighed the $650 billion plan, the $1 trillion projection, and the 82%/41% consensus against those lines.

An experienced analyst would log the ~$650 billion 2026 plan as the demand backdrop, footnote the $1 trillion as NVIDIA's slide, note consensus growth, and watch hyperscaler capex guidance plus Vera Rubin and H200-China milestones before betting on 2027.

question: Your answer opened one thesis on the big four hyperscalers' combined data-center capital expenditure for calendar 2026, and used the article's figure for calendar 2027 only as its reference. Why did you not open calendar 2027's combined spending as a thesis of its own?
reply:
I treated 2027 as the same aggregate, not a new question. Section 3 says “A thesis asks one quantity for one period,” and that “Another population or wording of the same aggregate is evidence for it”; it also bars opening a thesis for “another estimate, source or wording of what an open thesis tracks.” Nvidia's ~$1 trillion for next year is the same hyperscaler-capex quantity one year out, so it became the 2026 thesis's forward reference. I weighed those against “a quantity … for this or next calendar year” and “Do not exclude evidence solely because it concerns a related period,” which keep the 2027 figure as evidence rather than a second card.

An experienced analyst would record: ~$650bn of big-four 2026 capex plus Nvidia's ~$1trn 2027 projection as GPU-demand evidence; 82% and 41% consensus revenue growth as this year's/next year's earnings path; and drop the 5% share-price move, the 21.7x multiple and the “buy” conclusion as valuation, not research.

question: Your answer linked the report that NVIDIA has been negotiating to guarantee OpenAI's lease of a large Ohio data center to your candidate c1, on the amount of guarantees and credit support NVIDIA commits, and proposed no candidate on whether NVIDIA signs that guarantee by a check date. Why?
reply:
I linked the Ohio report to c1 because the instructions say an already-taken-on obligation “as one deal or as a programme” raises a financing_amount question, and that a candidate should cover the amount obligations reach at the next annual filing. The Ohio report describes negotiations, not an obligation already taken on.

The contrary instructions are explicit: “Not yet signed: a yes/no question due on a day after the item by which the signing can be checked, at most 18 months out.” The item says NVIDIA “has also recently been negotiating” to provide guarantees. That is a pending, checkable signing, so it should have prompted a yes/no binding_obligation candidate, due within 18 months—not been folded into c1’s financing_amount question.

An experienced analyst would treat the Ohio negotiations as material because the potential data center scale is stated and the proposed guarantee could create a major NVIDIA obligation. They would file it as evidence for a candidate asking whether NVIDIA signs the guarantee by a specified date, and not count it as an existing commitment in the annual-filing amount candidate.

question: Your answer linked the report that NVIDIA has been negotiating to guarantee OpenAI's lease of a large Ohio data center to your candidate c1, on the amount of guarantees and credit support NVIDIA commits, and proposed no candidate on whether NVIDIA signs that guarantee by a check date. Why?
reply:
I treated the reported negotiation as evidence for c1 because the instructions say an already-taken-on obligation is tracked by its financing amount at the next annual filing, and that “the announcement itself is evidence to it.” I also read the Ohio guarantee as another instance of the broader credit-support programme.

Against that, the candidate rules say: “Not yet signed: a yes/no question due on a day after the item by which the signing can be checked, at most 18 months out.” The article says NVIDIA was “negotiating to provide financial guarantees” for OpenAI’s lease, so this is a proposed, unsigned obligation—not merely an amount to track at the next filing. I should have proposed a separate yes/no binding-obligation candidate for whether NVIDIA signs the guarantee, with a check date within 18 months, and linked e6 to it. The amount candidate could still cover obligations already taken on.

An experienced analyst would flag the Ohio negotiation as a live contingent commitment risk, distinguish it from existing guarantees, and track whether it is signed rather than folding it only into an aggregate financing-amount question.
